GPT-5.5</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The causal chain that runs from weak antitrust to all sorts of social harms </span><em>necessarily runs through profits</em><span>. If companies aren’t making profit, they aren’t controlling the market. Yet Elizabeth Warren blamed high food prices on grocery stores’ market power during the post-pandemic inflation, despite the fact that these stores make very little profit, and their margins </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cd08ead0-9d88-443d-a836-644416d5db55?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">actually declined</a><span> as inflation accelerated. You could see that exact same misplaced focus in Lina Khan’s blockage of the Kroger/Albertsons merger. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As for airlines, the Biden administration’s blockage of the Spirit/JetBlue merger resulted in Spirit Airlines simply </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/424f1e0a-e62a-4520-baeb-1cc602c03d83?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">going out of business entirely</a><span>. Corporate concentration was achieved after all — but it was achieved with disorder, corporate failure, and 17,000 unemployed workers rather than with an orderly merger that would have preserved some of Spirit’s routes and workers. Not exactly a resounding success for the antimonopoly movement — but that’s what happens when you try to use antitrust tools against companies in low-margin industries. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Then there’s the case of housing. The antimonopoly people have eagerly embraced the idea that corporate landlords buying up rental properties and jacking up the price is a major cause of high rent. Democrats and Republicans have </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/23fa3296-003d-4692-9f5e-84ed866ae459?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">both embraced this piece of “slopulism”</a><span>, despite the fact that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45bd5adb-df3d-43ae-945d-311bfbc1c4f8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the percent of homes owned by corporate landlords is tiny</a><span> and there’s some evidence showing that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c6d081cc-1412-444e-904b-94b6075648a2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">corporate landlords tend to charge lower rents</a><span>. Supply constraints — failure to build more housing — is actually the reason for high rents, so the antimonopoly movement is distracting us from solving the real problem. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The movement’s obsessive monomania — its conviction that corporate concentration is the root of all of America’s problems — is causing it to pick the wrong targets and hurt workers. That doesn’t mean bigger corporations are better, or that there aren’t industries where we need stronger antitrust. But the antimonopolists’ totalizing obsession causes them to ignore the evidence of where and when their ideas are needed, because they assume that their ideas are </span><em>always</em><span> the top priority in every situation and should be applied in a blanket way to any target they choose. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The science on monopoly power isn’t settled</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Richard Feynman once said of science that “Of all its many values, the greatest must be the freedom to doubt.” Now you can respond that economics and politics aren’t “science”, but that makes the freedom to doubt even </span><em>more</em><span> important; the less conclusively that any one data set can answer your questions, the more important it is to look at a wide variety of data sets and consider a variety of explanations and theories. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">From Jonathan Chait’s description of Barry C. Lynn, he doesn’t seem like the kind of guy who’s inclined to look at evidence that goes against his ideas:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[Lynn] believes that “most prices are entirely arbitrary and political in nature.”…More expansively, Lynn believes that “market forces”—which he places in scare quotes—do not exist. His indictment of economics is neither mild nor limited. He has compared the discipline to Lysenkoism, a pseudo-scientific fad under Stalin. “The ‘science’ of economics today … ,” he wrote in his 2011 book, </span><em>Cornered</em><span>, “has become a form of madness, a dream of human imagination we mistake for a pattern of the world.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lina Khan </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/704af780-85dd-4a73-8331-32f4cd15d135?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">has also written</a><span> that “There are no such things as market ‘forces’.” Statements like this certainly don’t do much to refute Chait’s allegation that the antimonopoly belief system “is more like a religion than an economic theory”. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>First of all, as an aside, we should consider what it would mean for market forces not to exist and prices to be determined by politics. It would mean that grocery stores carefully calculate exactly how much they can charge for a cucumber or a package of napkins without Senators giving them an angry call or the working class rioting, or something like that. That’s kind of preposterous. It would also mean that small businesses would charge </span><em>lower</em><span> prices, because they’re less politically powerful than big businesses. But in fact, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/acc29bac-1ec9-44e6-87e9-782a1a840aef?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">it’s big businesses that charge lower prices</a><span> for the same goods. So the “prices are determined by politics” idea is just abjectly ridiculous, except maybe in a few special cases or where explicit regulation is involved. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But more to the point: Market forces obviously </span><em>do</em><span> exist. When you </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2baf9e86-1112-4ed1-b74c-ff841ffe3317?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">include sales taxes on price tags</a><span> — reminding people that prices are higher than they had thought — they buy less, proving that demand curves exist and slope downward. When there is bad weather at sea, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0d557df0-76da-40ee-96ab-1ba36afb4735?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the price of fish goes up</a><span>. When you charge electricity customers more, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6c770b05-5cee-41ee-86f2-5e0e797f8042?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">they use less electricity</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And so on. Market forces are not easy to observe in all cases, and they’re not always the most important determinant of prices. But their existence has been proven so thoroughly, by so much careful empirical observation, that to deny their existence requires a deep level of mysticism and blind faith. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">If you’re not the kind of person to believe in empirical economics, then of course you’re not going to care if economists find evidence against your worldview. But once we move out of the realm of willful faith-based belief and into the real world of evidence and observation, we find that the science on monopoly power is far from settled.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First of all, there is the evidence I cited before about decreasing concentration in local labor markets (even as concentration increases nationwide). The monopsony wage penalty might be very high, but it was probably even higher in the past; this leaves room for antitrust action to help workers, but it should make us question whether monopoly power is at the root of slow wage growth.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But more fundamentally, the entire story about creeping market power being responsible for a bunch of different ills in the modern American economy is </span><em>under serious dispute</em><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, the whole story about monopoly power increasing in recent decades relies on the idea that </span><em>price markups have increased</em><span> — if companies can’t charge higher prices relative to their costs, they must not be very powerful. Economists like De Loecker and Eeckhout find that markups have increased a lot, but there are plenty of economists who disagree with that finding! There are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c9ed95de-bf0d-4d06-936f-fd2afa0b4c4e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">tons of measurement issues</a><span> involved in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/72187044-a066-43e9-9426-77717799bdb4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">trying to estimate</a><span> markups across the whole economy. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dec05a58-f0d2-4aaf-bc36-2f5653273e09?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Some economists claim</a><span> that essentially the entire increase in markups is due to the finance sector. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are plenty of other pieces of the monopoly power story that are also disputed. </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a5e1fea2-7b08-4078-850e-897c1555a377?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Shapiro and Yurukoglu (2024)</a><span> summarize a bunch of these. It’s hard to define what each “market” is over time, because the boundaries of the categories are arbitrary, and the nature of products themselves keeps changing. It’s hard to choose the region over which local concentration should be measured (when is one store in the same “market” as another?). Companies’ costs are hard to measure for many reasons — for example, companies sell lots of different things, and researchers don’t necessarily have the data to determine which costs are for which products. Profits are hard to measure because the cost of risk is hard to assess. And so on. In general, choosing a different set of assumptions can get you wildly different results regarding how much monopoly power has actually risen in America.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The point here is not that De Loecker and Eeckhout, or the other economists who concluded in the 2010s that monopoly power is a big deal, were </span><em>wrong</em><span>. Maybe they were, maybe they weren’t. Nor should you conclude that economics is just a game of “he said, she said” where everyone contradicts each other and nobody really knows anything. The correct takeaway here is that these questions are very subtle and difficult, and the most careful, serious researchers will take a long time to hash out the correct answer. In the meantime, </span><strong>we must live with uncertainty</strong><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A big problem with the antimonopoly crusaders is that they don’t just refuse to live with uncertainty — they </span><em>insist that you don’t live with uncertainty</em><span> either. If you say “Hey dudes, maybe corporate landlords actually lower rents”, they won’t debate the finer points of causal estimation with you — they’ll simply label you as a corporate shill and dismiss you.</span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Don’t let the factionalists win</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s this last bit — the anathematization of anyone who disagrees with them — that really warns me away from the antimonopoly movement. Chait describes in his article how anyone who tries to buck the antimonopoly people gets accused of being a paid corporate hack:</p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“We’ve largely won the intellectual debate,” [Lynn] told me matter-of-factly, allowing that the only remaining liberals who disagree with him are “</span><strong>those who are paid to do so</strong><span>.”…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When Biden considered appointing Susan Davies, a former deputy White House counsel under President Obama, to the Justice Department’s top antitrust post, a </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cccbb869-bcce-4dd4-97f1-e5a564239eda?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">slew</a><span> of </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/959ac095-5ce4-4519-b913-af8e26947c67?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">articles</a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2733e8d8-ca9b-4230-9753-fa296e519b7d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">savaged</a><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b2484a16-5c33-472f-83ad-c658759be3d6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">her</a><span> as </span><strong>a corporate shill</strong><span>. Her candidacy died. [emphasis mine]</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This tactic was clearly on display when the antimonopoly people leapt to savage Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson’s book </span><em>Abundance</em><span>. Matt Stoller </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6f7ab530-73e8-4208-b7fa-b85d8276948a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">wrote a post</a><span> entitled “An Abundance of Sleaze: How a Beltway Brain Trust Sells Oligarchy to Liberals”. Dylan Gyauch-Lewis</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">¹</span><span> </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a0aa6ec7-52a8-4ad1-8e4a-87c4c3568141?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">called the Abundance movement</a><span> “The new centrist push to regain control of the Democratic Party, with corporate money”. Barry C. Lynn said that Abundance wants “to cozy up to good oligarchs, so they can shelter us until the MAGA storm blows over.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First of all, claiming that anyone who disagrees with your ideas must be on the payroll of nefarious forces is blatant intellectual dishonesty. It also signals how weak your argument is if you have to accuse every critic of being a bad actor. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But beyond that, the antimonopoly crusaders’ reaction to </span><em>Abundance</em><span> shows how utterly </span><em>factionalist</em><span> they are. They could have simply said “Yes, we want abundance too. Guess how you get abundance? By breaking up monopolies!” Or something like that. They could have easily tried to co-opt the energy behind </span><em>Abundance</em><span> and treated Ezra Klein and Derek Thompson as potential allies. Instead, they leapt instantly to the attack with maximum savagery. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the behavior of factionalists, for whom ideas and policy are less important than building power for a clique of favored allies and fellow-travelers within the Democratic Party. Klein and Thompson were a threat not because their ideas contradicted those of the antimonopoly clique, but simply because </span><em>they were not beholden</em><span> to the patronage or the intellectual legacy of that clique. They were not on the team, so they were the enemy. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In my view, it is very dangerous for any political party to allow itself to be entered and captured by a clique or faction like this. I’ve spent a long time being very favorable to the </span><em>ideas</em><span> being put forward by the antimonopoly people, but their </span><em>behavior</em><span> with regards to the Abundance liberals — and the shoddy reasoning, baseless accusations, and backroom arm-twisting that they employ in these debates — has given me what the Zoomers call “the ick”. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A problem with economic policy is that it is very vulnerable to </span><em>intellectual pseudo-cults</em><span>. Economics research is very hard to understand, isn’t always useful, and rarely offers clear-cut answers. So policymakers and writers seeking certainty and a reason for decisiveness often fall victim to charismatic gangs of intellectuals who claim that economics is solved and that they have it all figured out. On the GOP side, these include the “supply-siders” in the 1980s and the “national conservatives” today. On the Democratic side, it includes </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f0c4fb8f-2a76-437e-8fb9-b9ebb024ce3f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the MMT people</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But MMT failed — essentially no one listens to people who say infinite deficits are good. The antimonopoly faction, on the other hand, appears to have succeeded in winning enormous power and prestige within an increasingly epistemically closed progressive movement. Elizabeth Warren was basically a one-woman Organization Department</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">²</span><span> for the Biden administration, popular Democrats like AOC are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c0435c97-4adf-45cb-b32d-95b60c4819a8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">going around claiming</a><span> that “market power” is what produces billionaires, and every major progressive publication now platforms their intellectual output. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Given my writings about the problems of corporate power in the past — and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/45501f90-bb41-430d-86d1-1fd037c4c35f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">my fear of the overwhelming power</a><span> that AI companies might achieve — it would be relatively easy for me to join this movement. But I can’t, because monomaniacal obsession, epistemic closure, anti-empiricism, and intense factionalism are the kinds of things I just can’t sign on to. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Corporate power </span><em>is</em><span> a real problem in our society. But we need more reasonable programs, and more reasonable </span><em>people</em><span>, to fight it effectively. Banning corporate landlords, calling for </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/95a27648-963f-4cb8-b33d-e015c83c3fbb?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">price controls</a><span>, attacking the grocery store industry, forcing airlines out of business, and making accusations against anyone who calls for deregulation of housing supply are just signs of an approach that’s going to lead nowhere good. </span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height:
